purpose: Tiagabine is used to help control partial seizures in people with epilepsy. It is usually used alongside other seizure medications when seizures are not fully controlled on their own. Your doctor may prescribe it as part of your overall epilepsy treatment plan.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a natural calming chemical called GABA to help keep nerve activity balanced. In epilepsy, nerve signals can become overactive and cause seizures. Tiagabine works by slowing down the removal of GABA in the brain, so there is more of this calming chemical available to help prevent those overactive signals from turning into a seizure.
common_side_effects: You might feel dizzy, tired, or have trouble concentrating. Some people experience nervousness, shaking, or an upset stomach. Headaches and difficulty with memory or thinking clearly are also possible, especially when starting the medication.
warnings: This medication can cause seizures even in people who do not have epilepsy, especially if taken without other seizure medications or at higher doses than prescribed. It may cause serious mood changes, confusion, or in rare cases a severe condition where the brain experiences ongoing electrical activity without obvious seizures. Always take it with food and never stop it suddenly without talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor right away if you feel unusually depressed, confused, or have thoughts of harming yourself.
typical_dosing: Adults usually start at a low dose of 4 mg once a day and the dose is slowly increased over several weeks up to a typical range of 32 to 56 mg per day divided into 2 to 4 doses. It should always be taken with food to help reduce side effects. Your doctor will adjust the dose based on how well it works for you and how well you tolerate it.
